description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: A non-JSON Content-Type gets an undeclared 415 instead of the contract's 400 (or 413 when oversized)
findings.evidence: `SettingsBodyAdvice.beforeBodyRead` only runs after a JSON converter has accepted the request's media type. A PATCH sent as `text/plain` (or with no Content-Type) fails earlier with `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`. The global `SignInFailureAdvice` then turns that into Spring's standard 415. The contract (`contract/api/openapi.yaml:278-285`) declares only 200/400/413/422 for `updateProfileSettings`, and the spec says "bodies that are not a JSON object SHALL be 400" and "a body over 16 KB SHALL be 413". A 20 KB `text/plain` body gets 415, not 413. No profile test sends a non-JSON content type.
findings.suggestion: Either declare 415 in the docs-store contract for `updateProfileSettings`, or handle `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` for this endpoint in `ProfileProblemAdvice` (map it to `profile-settings-unreadable` 400, after the size check). Add a test that sends `text/plain`.

findings.title: A configured task locale longer than 16 characters passes validation, then fails on the DB write as a raw 500
findings.evidence: The column is `secondary_task_locale varchar(16)`. `TaskLocaleProperties.taskLocales` and `SettingsValidator` put no length limit on configured values: `if (field.value in supportedLocales) Change.To(field.value)`. If an operator configures a longer tag such as `zh-Hant-TW-x-private`, a valid PATCH reaches the flush inside `JpaChildProfileStore.updateSettings`. Postgres rejects the value, and the resulting `DataIntegrityViolationException` has no handler, so the client gets a 500. AGENTS.md says no input may produce a raw 500.
findings.suggestion: Validate `doucko.profile.task-locales` at startup: annotate the `@ConfigurationProperties` with `@Validated` and add a size/pattern check on each element of at most 16 characters, or refuse in `ProfileConfiguration`, so a bad configuration fails the start instead of a request.

findings.title: The display name is read through Environment, which resolves `${...}` placeholders in the value
findings.evidence: `environment.getProperty(DisplayNamePolicy.VARIABLE)` resolves nested placeholders. A value containing `${...}` is either silently replaced with the resolved text (a different name is stored) or throws `IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder '...' in value "..."`. That exception message quotes the raw value, so the startup failure log would contain part of the name. This bypasses the DisplayNamePolicy guarantee that refusals name the variable and never the value (NFR-3).
findings.suggestion: Read the raw value without placeholder resolution, e.g. `System.getenv(VARIABLE)` with the test property-source fallback, or iterate `ConfigurableEnvironment.propertySources` and call `getProperty` on the source directly. Add a test with a value containing `${x}`.

findings.title: The control-character rule allows line/paragraph separators and bidi-override characters
findings.evidence: The check is `Character.getType(it) == Character.CONTROL.toInt()`, which covers category Cc only. U+2028/U+2029 (Zl/Zp) break lines like a newline, and U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE (Cf) reorders displayed text. All three are accepted and stored, and the name will be rendered in the UI. The spec rejects newlines because they are line breaks, so it likely wants these refused too.
findings.suggestion: Also refuse `LINE_SEPARATOR`, `PARAGRAPH_SEPARATOR` and `FORMAT` (Cf) code points, or at least the bidi controls U+202A–U+202E and U+2066–U+2069, if the store spec agrees. Add golden cases to `DisplayNamePolicyTest`.

findings.title: The controller ignores the generated body parameter and depends on a hidden request attribute; a missing attribute is a raw 500
findings.evidence: `updateProfileSettings` discards `profileSettingsPatch`. It fetches the request through `RequestContextHolder` and calls `SettingsBodyAdvice.input(request)`, which is `checkNotNull(request.getAttribute(INPUT) as? SettingsInput)`. The attribute is set only if `SettingsBodyAdvice.supports` matched. Any path where the advice is skipped throws `IllegalStateException`, which nothing maps, so the client gets a 500. Examples: a converter other than Jackson reading the DTO, or a refactor that changes the parameter type. The coupling is invisible from the controller signature.
findings.suggestion: Map a missing input to `UnreadableSettingsException` (400) instead of `checkNotNull`. Prefer an injected `HttpServletRequest` parameter or a small `HandlerMethodArgumentResolver` for `SettingsInput` over the static `RequestContextHolder` lookup.

findings.title: Coverage summary: 11 change-spec scenarios: 10 implemented, 1 partial, 0 missing, 0 contradicted. The in-scope store-spec scenarios add 2 more partials (UTF-8 bytes, container restart).
findings.evidence: Implemented with tests: First start trims the name (ChildProfileStartupTest/IT); Restart keeps the profile and its settings (ChildProfileStartupIT:92); Fifty code points accepted (ChildProfileStartupIT:128); Defaults, set and clear; Omitted and unknown fields; Validation wins over GUIDED; GUIDED discards the whole request; Oversized locale not echoed; Empty configuration (ProfileSettingsTest:83-317); Log capture (ProfileSettingsIT:98, ChildProfileStartupIT). Partial: Invalid names refuse to start, because a placeholder-shaped value leaks (see the separate finding). Store-spec scenarios that need HQ, XP, e2e, the privacy scan or recordings are listed under 'Scope NOT delivered' in docs/current-state.md and the design Non-goals, so they are deferred and not missing.
findings.suggestion: No action for this entry. It only records the coverage line the output contract asks for.

findings.title: The display name is read through Spring's placeholder-resolving Environment, so a value containing '${' can be echoed in the startup error or silently replaced
findings.evidence: Spec: 'the startup SHALL fail ... with a message that names DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME and the rule and never the value'. Store spec: 'the printed error ... contains neither Hrdinka nor the x run'. Code: `DisplayNamePolicy.check(environment.getProperty(DisplayNamePolicy.VARIABLE))`. `PropertyResolver.getProperty` resolves nested placeholders. With a value like `Ann${x}`, it throws a PlaceholderResolutionException whose message quotes the whole value (`Could not resolve placeholder 'x' in value "Ann${x}"`). Spring Boot logs that message as 'Application run failed', which is an NFR-3 leak. With a value like `Ann${HOME}`, a different name is stored without any error. No test covers placeholder syntax.
findings.suggestion: Read the raw value without placeholder resolution. Options: `System.getenv(VARIABLE)` behind an injectable supplier, or `(environment as ConfigurableEnvironment).propertySources` with direct lookup in the systemEnvironment source. Add a DisplayNamePolicy or startup test where the variable is `Hrdinka${nope}`: the refusal and the captured output must not contain it, or the value must be stored verbatim.

findings.title: Task 5.4 (compose smoke) is ticked but was skipped and has no artifact
findings.evidence: tasks.md reads `- [x] 5.4 Smoke through 127.0.0.1:8081 (GET, PATCH uk, PATCH GUIDED 422). SKIPPED 2026-10-04 ...`. No smoke evidence file exists (slice 2 had docs/qa/evidence/slice2-compose-smoke.md; slice 4 has none). The store-spec scenario 'Setting survives a backend restart' (WHEN 'the backend containers restart') is covered only by in-process context restarts in ChildProfileStartupIT, not by a container restart.
findings.suggestion: Untick 5.4, or mark it explicitly as a waiver rather than done, until the smoke runs. Then run it on a free stack, including a `docker compose restart backend` followed by GET, and record docs/qa/evidence/slice4-compose-smoke.md.

findings.title: The invalid UTF-8 scenario is tested only with a literal U+FFFD string, never with the byte sequence 0xC3 0x28
findings.evidence: Store spec scenario 'Name that is not valid UTF-8 is refused': 'GIVEN ... the display-name variable containing the byte sequence 0xC3 0x28 (invalid UTF-8) ... THEN it exits with a non-zero status'. The implementation relies on the JVM decoding the environment bytes to U+FFFD (DisplayNamePolicy.kt:33, comment line 49). The tests inject a Kotlin string that already contains U+FFFD, so the actual env-decoding path (sun.jnu.encoding in the container) is never exercised.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that launches the JVM (ProcessBuilder or a Testcontainers backend image) with raw env bytes C3 28, and assert a non-zero exit, the variable name in the output, and no row. If that is impractical, document the assumption (UTF-8 jnu encoding in eclipse-temurin) in design.md and record it as a waiver.

findings.title: Configured task locales are not validated against the contract shape or the column width
findings.evidence: openapi.yaml ProfileSettings/ProfileSettingsPatch: `secondaryTaskLocale: pattern: ^[a-z]{2}$`. Code: `data class TaskLocaleProperties(val taskLocales: List<String> = emptyList())` has no validation, and V1__child_profile.sql has `secondary_task_locale varchar(16)`. A configured value such as `uk-UA` would be accepted and returned in a 200 that violates the contract pattern. A value over 16 characters would cause a DB error on PATCH, which is a raw 500.
findings.suggestion: Validate `doucko.profile.task-locales` at startup (each entry matches ^[a-z]{2}$, otherwise refuse to start), with a unit test. Alternatively, amend the contract description.

findings.title: The unknown answer-mode message tells the child to use GUIDED, which is always refused
findings.evidence: Store spec: '`answerMode`: ... in MVP only `DIRECT` is accepted'; 'GUIDED SHALL be refused as not available yet (422)'. Code: `profile.field.UNKNOWN_VALUE=Use DIRECT or GUIDED.` The 400 `errors[].message` for `SOCRATIC`/`direct` steers the client to a value that is then answered 422.
findings.suggestion: Change the message to 'Use DIRECT.' (or 'DIRECT; GUIDED is not available yet'), and assert the text in ProfileSettingsTest.

findings.title: The schema and the persistence enum allow GUIDED to be stored, while the spec says no other value can be stored
findings.evidence: Store spec exclusions: '`answerMode` ... while it is `DIRECT`, and no other value can be stored.' The migration has `CHECK (answer_mode IN ('DIRECT', 'GUIDED'))`. Only ProfileSettingsService.kt:316 enforces DIRECT-only; there is no persistence-level guard. This is a deliberate forward-compatibility choice, but it is not recorded as a requirement or design decision in the change spec.
findings.suggestion: Record the choice in design.md (the schema is ready for later phases; the service is the single enforcement point). Alternatively, restrict the CHECK to 'DIRECT' and widen it in a later append-only migration.

findings.title: An undocumented hardening change in the shared log guard (org.hibernate.validator capped) has no requirement in the change spec
findings.evidence: The diff adds `"org.hibernate.validator"` to the capped loggers in the shared module. The change spec and proposal mention only extending the NFR-3 log-capture test, not changing shared logging policy. The RED-run evidence (slice4-red-run.md) shows this fixed a real TRACE-level leak, so the change is justified.
findings.suggestion: Add a line to proposal.md 'What Changes' or design.md that names the shared log-guard change under NFR-3, so the platform-foundation logging policy stays traceable.

result.reasoning: Confirmed, with corrections to the details. SettingsBodyAdvice.kt has only 113 lines, so line 321 is wrong. The behaviour is still real. The generated `ChildProfileApi.kt:52` declares `consumes = ["application/json"]` on the mapping. So a PATCH sent as `text/plain`, or with no Content-Type, fails at handler mapping: RequestMappingInfoHandlerMapping throws HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException before the controller is chosen or the body is read. The 16 KB check in SettingsBodyAdvice.beforeBodyRead (lines 50-52) and the not-a-JSON-object check never run. The global SignInFailureAdvice (`@Order(HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)`, catching HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException) only special-cases `POST /api/admin/session`. For every other path it hands the exception to the standard ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, which returns 415. The contract for updateProfileSettings (`contract/api/openapi.yaml:272-285`) lists only 200/400/422/413. The store spec (`child-profile/spec.md:247-258`) says invalid PATCHes use the status codes from openapi.yaml. So a 415 is undeclared, and a 20 KB text/plain body gets 415 instead of 413. No src test mentions 415 or text/plain. Severity minor is right: it is still an RFC 7807 problem, not a 500, so nothing leaks. The suggested fix needs a correction. Because the 415 is raised during handler mapping, there is no handler yet. `ProfileProblemAdvice(assignableTypes = [ProfileSettingsController])` would never see it. The fix has to go in the global advice, switched on the path (like SignInFailureAdvice), or the contract has to declare 415.

I could not refute this. The mechanism holds, though the cited line is wrong: SettingsBodyAdvice.kt has only 114 lines, and the size and JSON checks are at lines 50–52 and 69–80.

How it happens:
- `SettingsBodyAdvice` is a `RequestBodyAdviceAdapter`. Spring only calls `beforeBodyRead`/`handleEmptyBody` after a message converter has accepted the request's media type for `ProfileSettingsPatch`.
- A PATCH sent as `text/plain`, or with no Content-Type (Spring treats that as `application/octet-stream`), fails earlier with `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException`. That happens whether it is raised at handler mapping (if the generated interface declares `consumes = application/json`) or at converter selection.
- Nothing in profile handles that exception. Searching src/main finds it only in `SignInFailureAdvice` (admin), which is global and `HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE`. For any request that is not POST /api/admin/session, it falls through to `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler.handleException`, which returns the standard 415.
- No global body-size filter exists. 413 is produced only by `SettingsBodyAdvice` via `ProfileProblemAdvice`. So a 20 KB `text/plain` body gets 415, not 413.
- Contract openapi.yaml:266–285 declares only 200/400/422/413 for `updateProfileSettings`, so 415 is undeclared.

Anyone can reproduce this with curl. Impact is low, though: the response is still a clean RFC 7807 problem, not a raw 500. Nothing leaks, and the real frontend always sends JSON. It is a contract/spec mismatch, so "minor" is right.

The mechanism holds. `TaskLocaleProperties` (`application/TaskLocaleProperties.kt:9-12`) is a plain `@ConfigurationProperties` class. It has no `@Validated` and no constraint on its elements. `ProfileSettingsService` (`ProfileSettingsService.kt:20-22`) uses the configured list as-is for `SettingsValidator`. The validator (`domain/SettingsPatch.kt:97`) accepts any submitted value that exactly matches a configured locale and does no length or format check. The column is `secondary_task_locale varchar(16)` (`V1__child_profile.sql:10`). Postgres raises a "value too long" error for a longer string, which reaches the app as a `DataIntegrityViolationException`. None of the advice classes handle it: `ProfileProblemAdvice` handles only `InvalidSettings`, `UnreadableSettings`, `GuidedModeNotAvailable` and `SettingsBodyTooLarge`, and `SignInFailureAdvice` covers admin sign-in only. So a PATCH carrying a configured locale longer than 16 characters ends in a raw 500. Mitigating factors: only operator misconfiguration can trigger it, not ordinary user input, and the shipped config is `task-locales: uk`. It is a latent issue, so minor severity fits.

The mechanism is real but no user or attacker can trigger it. These parts check out: `V1__child_profile.sql:10` declares `secondary_task_locale varchar(16)`. `TaskLocaleProperties` is an unvalidated `List<String>`. `ProfileSettingsService` only uses `locales.taskLocales.distinct()` as the allow-list. `ProfileProblemAdvice` has no `DataIntegrityViolationException` handler, and no other advice does either.

But a client can only send a value that is already in the operator-configured allow-list. Any other value is rejected first by `SettingsValidator`. The only configured value is `task-locales: uk` in `application.yaml:67`, which is 2 characters. So with the shipped configuration, no request can reach the overflow.

Triggering it would take an operator deliberately setting a locale tag of 17 or more characters. Real BCP-47 task locales like `uk`, `en-GB` or `zh-Hant-TW` all fit. That is a deployment misconfiguration, not "user input producing a raw 500" as AGENTS.md defines it. Seen as exploitable or reproducible by a real user or attacker, the finding does not hold.

Checking the configuration at startup would still be reasonable hardening. If kept at all, it should be a nit about configuration robustness, not a correctness defect.

I could not refute this finding. At `ChildProfileInitializer.kt:19` the code calls `environment.getProperty(DisplayNamePolicy.VARIABLE)` on a Spring `Environment`. That call goes through `PropertySourcesPropertyResolver.getProperty(key, String.class, resolveNestedPlaceholders = true)`, so Spring resolves placeholders inside the value before `DisplayNamePolicy.check` ever sees it.

There are two ways this goes wrong:
- **Resolvable placeholder:** a value like `${HOME}` is silently replaced by the resolved text, and that different name is stored.
- **Unresolvable placeholder:** `ignoreUnresolvableNestedPlaceholders` is false by default, so `resolveRequiredPlaceholders` throws `IllegalArgumentException` (`PlaceholderResolutionException` in Spring 6.2+). Its message is `Could not resolve placeholder 'x' in value "<raw value>"`. Spring Boot logs this when startup fails, so part of the name ends up in the log, which goes against NFR-3.

Nothing guards against this. `DisplayNamePolicy` only checks for a missing value, length, control characters and UTF-8, and it runs after resolution has already happened.

The trigger is unlikely: a child's display name containing `${` is rare and set by the operator. So confidence low and severity minor are reasonable, but the mechanism is real.

The mechanism is real. `ChildProfileInitializer.kt:19` calls `environment.getProperty(DisplayNamePolicy.VARIABLE)`. In Spring's `AbstractEnvironment`, this goes through `PropertySourcesPropertyResolver.getProperty(key, String, resolveNestedPlaceholders=true)`, so `${...}` inside the value gets resolved. Spring Boot does not turn on `ignoreUnresolvableNestedPlaceholders` by default. So a value like `${x}` either resolves silently to other text or throws `PlaceholderResolutionException`/IAE, and that exception message quotes the raw value ("Could not resolve placeholder 'x' in value \"...\""). Nothing in the code reads the raw value first: `DisplayNamePolicy.check` only sees the already-resolved string, and none of its violations (MISSING/TOO_LONG/CONTROL_CHARACTER/NOT_UTF8) applies before resolution. So I can't refute it on the mechanism.

The real-world risk is close to zero, though:
(1) The value comes only from the operator's own env/.env (`DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME`) and is read once, on first start. No HTTP request or child input reaches this path, so there is no attacker.
(2) To trigger it, a parent would have to deliberately type `${` into their child's display name. That is not a realistic name.
(3) If docker compose supplies the env, compose already interpolates `${...}` in .env/env_file values before Spring sees them, which hides the case further.
(4) The worst outcome is a fragment of the name in the operator's own startup log on their own machine. Nothing crosses a trust boundary.

The fix is cheap and reasonable as a hardening step: read through `System.getenv` or the raw property source. Keep it as a minor/nit hardening item, not a correctness or privacy defect.

The finding is right about what the code does: line 34 (the finding says 36) only checks Character.CONTROL, which is category Cc, so U+2028, U+2029 and U+202E get through. That is still not a correctness defect. The behaviour was chosen on purpose and is written down. design.md decision 6 says "no control characters (category Cc) and no U+FFFD", and the KDoc on the policy says "no control character (category Cc)". The store spec says "no control character" and its scenario lists only newline, tab and U+FFFD, all of which the code refuses. Zl and Zp are not control characters in Unicode terms. Cf is "format", not "control". So the code does what the spec and design say. The rest of the finding is a guess ("the spec … likely wants these refused"), not a demonstrated bug.

The input also limits the impact. The name comes only from the DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME environment variable, which the operator sets in .env. It is read once, on the first start, from an empty database. No request can set it, so there is no attacker-controlled path for bidi spoofing. Rendering is the frontend's job, and React escapes text, so a U+2028 in a text node does not break any markup. At most this is a suggestion to tighten the spec in the docs store first. It is not a mechanism that is wrong in this code.

The mechanism is real: `Character.getType(...) == CONTROL` (`DisplayNamePolicy.kt:34`) only matches category Cc, so U+2028, U+2029 and U+202E would get through. But from an exploitability point of view, nobody can trigger this as an attacker.

1. **Only the operator sets the input.** The value comes from the `DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME` environment variable, which the person running the deployment puts in `.env` before the first start. The messages say so. No child or other untrusted user can submit it. The only person who could put a bidi override or line separator into the name is the trusted admin/parent who also controls the whole server, so this is not a security boundary.
2. **The code matches the spec.** `design.md:67` says "no control characters (category Cc) and no U+FFFD", and the KDoc repeats it. The spec scenario (`spec.md:33`) lists only newline, tab and U+FFFD as refused. Refusing Zl/Zp/Cf would go beyond the spec. Even the finding says the spec only "likely wants" it, and the confidence is low.
3. **The worst case is cosmetic and self-inflicted.** The operator's own child's name would show reversed or across two lines in their own UI. Blocking all Cf code points could also wrongly refuse legitimate names that use ZWJ/ZWNJ (also Cf).

This is at most a possible spec improvement, not a defect a real user or attacker can exploit.

I couldn't find any request that reaches the handler without the attribute set, so the claimed 500 doesn't happen in the current code.

- **The advice runs for every converter.** `SettingsBodyAdvice.supports` (SettingsBodyAdvice.kt:42) checks only `methodParameter.parameterType == ProfileSettingsPatch::class.java`. It ignores `converterType`. So the finding's first example, "a converter other than Jackson reading the DTO", doesn't skip the advice. Spring's `AbstractMessageConverterMethodArgumentResolver` calls `beforeBodyRead` for whichever converter `canRead` the body.
- **Every outcome of `beforeBodyRead` is safe.** It either stores the parsed `SettingsInput` or throws one of its own mapped exceptions: `SettingsBodyTooLargeException` (413) or `UnreadableSettingsException` (400).
- **Empty bodies are covered.** An empty body either fails to parse (null tree → `UnreadableSettingsException`) or goes to `handleEmptyBody`, which throws the same exception.
- **No converter means no handler call.** If no converter can read the content type, Spring throws `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` (415) before the handler is invoked.

So whenever `updateProfileSettings` actually runs, the attribute is present. `checkNotNull` is an invariant assertion, not a reachable error path.

The finding's second example, "a refactor that changes the parameter type", is a maintainability concern about something that might break later. It isn't a correctness defect in this code. The class KDoc and the controller comment both document the coupling. The suggestion to inject `HttpServletRequest` or use an argument resolver is a style point, not a fix for a live bug.

I could not find a way for a real client to make the handler run without the attribute set. In Spring MVC, the `@RequestBody` resolver (`AbstractMessageConverterMethodArgumentResolver`) applies the `RequestBodyAdvice` chain to every converter that can read the target type. `SettingsBodyAdvice.supports` checks only that the parameter type is `ProfileSettingsPatch`, so the converter in use does not matter.

That leaves three request shapes, and each one is covered:
- **Non-empty body:** `beforeBodyRead` always runs. It either sets INPUT or throws `SettingsBodyTooLargeException` (413) or `UnreadableSettingsException` (400).
- **Empty body:** `handleEmptyBody` throws `UnreadableSettingsException`.
- **Content type no converter can read:** Spring throws `HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException` (415) before the handler is called.

So the handler only runs after INPUT has been set, and the `checkNotNull` failure cannot happen at runtime. The finding's own examples (a refactor that changes the parameter type, or a different setup) are hypothetical future code changes, not anything a user or attacker can trigger. What remains is a maintainability point about hidden coupling, not a reachable 500.

I confirmed the mechanism in the code. ChildProfileInitializer.kt:19 reads the name with `environment.getProperty(DisplayNamePolicy.VARIABLE)`. Spring's `AbstractEnvironment.getProperty` delegates to a property resolver that resolves nested placeholders by default. `ignoreUnresolvableNestedPlaceholders` defaults to false, so `resolveRequiredPlaceholders` runs. That has two effects:
(a) If the value contains an unresolvable `${x}`, `getProperty` throws a PlaceholderResolutionException whose message quotes the whole raw value (for example `Could not resolve placeholder 'x' in value "Ann${x}"`). This happens before DisplayNamePolicy.check runs, so the policy's careful never-print-the-value messages are bypassed, and Spring Boot logs the exception as 'Application run failed'.
(b) If the value contains a resolvable `${HOME}` or similar, the name is silently substituted. DisplayNamePolicy only checks blankness, U+FFFD, control characters and length, so a value like `Ann${USER}` would be accepted and stored with the substitution.
Nothing guards against this elsewhere. No test uses `$` or `{` in the name, and DisplayNamePolicy cannot intervene because resolution happens first. So the spec breach is real ("never the value", "contains neither Hrdinka nor the x run").

Exploitability is low, though. The only person who can set DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME is the operator or parent configuring .env. A child's display name containing `${` is very unlikely in practice. The leaked value goes only to the operator's own startup console, which the operator already has. No remote attacker can influence the value or trigger the path. The issue is real and reproducible, but it is a correctness and spec-compliance defect with negligible real-world impact, not a major security issue. I recommend downgrading the severity.
